episode_title: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product-Market Fit
summary: Rahul Vohra shares his quantitative methodology for measuring, reverse-engineering, and optimizing product-market fit (PMF) using Sean Ellis's 40% benchmark, segmenting high-expectation customers, and balancing bug fixes with high-impact feature development.
transcript:
Lenny Rachitsky: Welcome to the podcast, Rahul. Today we're diving deep into product-market fit. Most founders treat PMF as this binary, mystical event—either you have it or you don't. But at Superhuman, you turned finding product-market fit into a repeatable, quantitative engine. How did that begin?

Rahul Vohra: Thanks Lenny. In 2017, we were two years into building Superhuman. We had rebuilt the app from scratch, but I felt immense anxiety because I couldn't answer the simplest question: 'Do we have product-market fit?' The classic definitions—like Marc Andreessen's 'the customers are buying products as fast as you can make them'—are completely useless when you're pre-launch. You cannot manage what you cannot measure.

So I discovered Sean Ellis's benchmark. Sean had analyzed hundreds of startups and found a leading indicator: ask your users, 'How would you feel if you could no longer use the product?' with options: 'Very disappointed', 'Somewhat disappointed', and 'Not disappointed'. Sean found that if 40% or more say 'Very disappointed', the company tends to achieve hyper-growth. Below 40%, companies almost invariably struggle to grow sustainably.

Lenny Rachitsky: When you first ran that survey across Superhuman's early users, what was your score?

Rahul Vohra: In summer 2017, our score was only 22%. It was a gut punch. Less than a quarter of our users would be very disappointed if we shut down tomorrow. But the breakthrough wasn't just knowing the score—it was realizing we could create an engine to systematically move that number from 22% to 40% and beyond.

Lenny Rachitsky: What was the 4-step process in that engine?

Rahul Vohra: Step 1 is Segmenting to find your High-Expectation Customer (HXC). When we looked at the 22% who loved us, they weren't random. They were founders, executives, lawyers, investors—people whose entire day is spent in email. When we filtered the dataset to people who said email was critical to their job, our PMF score instantly jumped from 22% to 32%.

Step 2 is Analyzing the Feedback. We asked: 'What is the main benefit you receive from Superhuman?' For our 'Very disappointed' users, the answer was speed, keyboard shortcuts, and email triage. Then we asked the 'Somewhat disappointed' cohort: 'What is the main thing holding you back?' Here's the critical nuance: we threw away the feedback from people who answered 'Not disappointed'—they will pull your product in the wrong direction.

Step 3 is Building the Roadmap by doubling down on what lovers love, while addressing what holds back the on-the-fence users. We allocated our engineering resources 50/50: 50% on doubling down on speed, offline mode, and shortcuts, and 50% on addressing high-leverage objections from the somewhat disappointed group—namely mobile apps and calendar integration.

Lenny Rachitsky: And what happened to the score after running that loop?

Rahul Vohra: Within three quarters, our PMF score rose from 22% to 33%, then to 46%, and eventually crossed 58%. It gave our entire team complete conviction to launch. Product-market fit is not an emotional gut feeling—it is an engineering discipline.
